concepts.title: Objectives of the Government Budget: Allocation, Redistribution, Stabilisation
concepts.definition: Through its budget the government directs resources toward goods markets fail to supply, reshapes the income distribution via taxes and transfers, and leans against booms and slumps by managing aggregate demand.
concepts.key_idea: The budget is the state's instrument for supplying public goods, evening out incomes and steadying the economy.
question_patterns: name the three functions a government budget performs
how does the budget redistribute income among households
explain the stabilisation role of government spending and taxation
why must the state allocate resources to some goods itself
show how taxes and transfers change personal disposable income
when would the government act to raise or restrain aggregate demand

solution_steps.explain: Defence, roads and administration would be undersupplied by markets, so budgetary finance must provide them.
Progressive taxation and transfer payments shift purchasing power toward groups society judges to need it.
Because wages and prices adjust slowly, the government expands demand in slumps and restrains it in inflationary booms.

concepts.title: Public Goods versus Private Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
concepts.definition: A public good is consumed jointly - one person's enjoyment does not diminish another's, and nobody can be barred from its benefits - so non-payers ride free and private firms will not supply it, leaving provision to the government budget.
concepts.key_idea: Non-rivalry and non-excludability break the payment link, so markets starve public goods and the state must step in.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.1.1, public goods discussion and free riders, page 67
question_patterns: why must public goods be provided by the government rather than private firms
state the two features that set public goods apart from private goods
explain the free rider problem with an example
why can no one be excluded from the benefits of a public park or clean air
contrast rivalry and excludability for a shirt and for street lighting
distinguish public provision of a good from public production of it

solution_steps.explain: If one person's use leaves less for others, the good is a private one; shared benefits at full availability mark a public good.
Where collecting fees from every beneficiary is impossible, non-payers cannot be kept out.
Free riders break the producer-consumer payment link, so the budget finances the good even though private agents may help produce it.

concepts.title: Revenue Receipts: Tax and Non-Tax Revenue
concepts.definition: Receipts that create no claim on the government are revenue receipts; they comprise tax revenue - direct taxes on incomes and profits plus indirect taxes on goods and services - and non-tax items such as interest, dividends, fees and grants received.
concepts.key_idea: If a receipt neither borrows nor sells assets, it is revenue, whether taxed or earned.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.1.2, revenue receipts classification, pages 68-69
question_patterns: classify government receipts into tax and non-tax revenue with examples
how do direct taxes differ from indirect taxes
why are revenue receipts called non-redeemable
list the sources of non-tax revenue of the central government
place excise duty customs duty and corporation tax in the right category
which receipts of the government create no liability and reduce no assets

solution_steps.explain: A receipt that neither creates a repayment obligation nor lowers an asset is a revenue receipt.
Direct taxes fall on incomes and firm profits; indirect taxes such as GST, excise and customs ride on goods and services.
Interest on government loans, dividends, fees, fines and foreign grants complete revenue receipts.

concepts.title: Capital Receipts: Debt-Creating and Non-Debt-Creating
concepts.definition: Receipts that either build a repayment obligation or shrink the government's assets are capital receipts: borrowings create future liability, while recovery of loans and sale of PSU shares merely reduce financial assets without borrowing.
concepts.key_idea: Any receipt that raises a liability or sells off an asset is capital, and only the borrowing part creates debt.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.1.2, capital receipts paragraph, page 69
question_patterns: what makes a receipt a capital receipt
why does borrowing create a liability while disinvestment does not
classify recovery of loans and sale of PSU shares as capital receipts
which capital receipts add to government debt and which do not
give examples of non-debt creating capital receipts
how does selling a government asset affect future earnings

solution_steps.explain: Fresh borrowing must be repaid with interest, so it is a debt-creating capital receipt.
Loan recoveries and PSU disinvestment bring in cash by shrinking financial assets, not by borrowing.
Capital receipts split into debt-creating (borrowings) and non-debt-creating (recoveries, disinvestment) - a split that matters for the fiscal deficit.

concepts.title: Revenue Expenditure versus Capital Expenditure
concepts.definition: Spending that neither builds any asset nor cuts a liability - salaries, subsidies, interest, grants - is revenue expenditure, while outlays that create assets such as land, buildings and machinery or that repay liabilities are capital expenditure.
concepts.key_idea: Ask whether the outlay leaves behind an asset or removes a liability; if not, it is revenue spending.
question_patterns: separate revenue expenditure from capital expenditure with examples
why are interest payments counted as revenue expenditure
is a loan given to a state government revenue or capital spending
which expenditure builds assets for the government
classify salaries subsidies and land purchase into the two heads
how does the asset-creation test sort government spending

solution_steps.explain: Outlays on land, buildings, machinery, shares and loans advanced create assets, so they are capital expenditure.
Repaying past loans lowers liabilities and therefore also counts as capital expenditure.
Day-to-day running costs, interest due, subsidies and most grants create no asset, so they are revenue expenditure.

concepts.title: Balanced, Surplus and Deficit Budget
concepts.definition: Matching total spending with total receipts balances the budget; receipts above spending leave a surplus, and the common case of spending above receipts is a deficit that must be met by borrowing.
concepts.key_idea: The sign of receipts minus spending labels the budget as balanced, surplus or deficit.
question_patterns: define balanced surplus and deficit budgets
find whether a budget is in surplus or deficit from receipts and spending
what does a zero budget balance signify
compute the budget balance when revenue and capital figures are given
which budget situation forces the government to borrow
why is the deficit the most common budgetary position

solution_steps.explain: Subtracting total expenditure from total receipts gives the budget balance.
A positive balance is a surplus, zero is balanced, and a negative balance is a deficit equal to the borrowing need.

worked_examples.question: Using Balanced, Surplus and Deficit Budget, compute the result for total_receipts = 3, total_expenditure = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Net receipts against spending: budget_balance = total_receipts - total_expenditure = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Balanced, Surplus and Deficit Budget, compute the result for total_receipts = 4, total_expenditure = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Net receipts against spending: budget_balance = total_receipts - total_expenditure = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Revenue Deficit
concepts.definition: The gap by which revenue expenditure outruns revenue receipts is the revenue deficit; it shows the government is dissaving and borrowing to fund everyday consumption rather than asset creation.
concepts.key_idea: A revenue deficit means borrowed money is financing consumption, a warning about expenditure quality.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.2.1, revenue deficit and Table 5.1, pages 71-72
question_patterns: compute the revenue deficit from revenue receipts and revenue expenditure
what does a rising revenue deficit indicate about government borrowing
why is a revenue deficit a sign of government dissaving
revenue expenditure is 11.8 and receipts 9.2 percent of GDP, find the revenue deficit
how does the revenue deficit differ from the fiscal deficit
which deficit shows borrowing used for consumption rather than investment

solution_steps.action: Subtract current receipts from current spending
solution_steps.explain: Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts isolates the shortfall on the current account of the budget.

worked_examples.question: Using Revenue Deficit, compute the result for revenue_expenditure = 3, revenue_receipts = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Subtract current receipts from current spending: revenue_deficit = revenue_expenditure - revenue_receipts = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Revenue Deficit, compute the result for revenue_expenditure = 4, revenue_receipts = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Subtract current receipts from current spending: revenue_deficit = revenue_expenditure - revenue_receipts = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Fiscal Deficit as the Borrowing Requirement
concepts.definition: Total expenditure minus all receipts other than borrowings is the fiscal deficit, which measures exactly how much the government must borrow from all sources - the public, the RBI and abroad.
concepts.key_idea: Strip out borrowings from receipts and the residual gap is precisely the borrowing requirement.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.2.1, fiscal deficit and financing side, page 72
question_patterns: calculate the fiscal deficit from total expenditure and non-borrowed receipts
why does the fiscal defect equal the government's borrowing requirement
which receipts are excluded while measuring the fiscal deficit
find the financing-side composition of the fiscal deficit from home and foreign borrowing
total spending is 15, revenue receipts 9.2 and non-debt capital receipts 0.2, compute the fiscal deficit
how does the fiscal deficit relate to the revenue deficit and capital spending

solution_steps.action: Add up receipts that create no debt
solution_steps.explain: Revenue receipts plus recoveries of loans and disinvestment proceeds form non-borrowed receipts.
Total expenditure minus non-borrowed receipts is the fiscal deficit, financed by net home borrowing, RBI borrowing and foreign borrowing.

worked_examples.question: Using Fiscal Deficit as the Borrowing Requirement, compute the result for revenue_receipts = 3, recovery_of_loans = 3, disinvestment_proceeds = 3, total_expenditure = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add up receipts that create no debt: non_borrowed_receipts = revenue_receipts + recovery_of_loans + disinvestment_proceeds = 9.0 Step 2: Gap total spending against them: fiscal_deficit = total_expenditure - non_borrowed_receipts = -7.0 Final result: -7.0

worked_examples.question: Using Fiscal Deficit as the Borrowing Requirement, compute the result for revenue_receipts = 4, recovery_of_loans = 4, disinvestment_proceeds = 4, total_expenditure = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add up receipts that create no debt: non_borrowed_receipts = revenue_receipts + recovery_of_loans + disinvestment_proceeds = 12.0 Step 2: Gap total spending against them: fiscal_deficit = total_expenditure - non_borrowed_receipts = -9.0 Final result: -9.0

concepts.title: Primary Deficit
concepts.definition: Removing interest obligations on past debt from the fiscal deficit leaves the primary deficit, which isolates the borrowing caused by this year's spending decisions alone.
concepts.key_idea: The primary deficit separates today's fiscal imbalance from the legacy cost of yesterday's debt.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, section 5.2.1, primary deficit paragraph, page 73
question_patterns: work out the primary deficit from the fiscal deficit and interest payments
why do we deduct interest to obtain the primary deficit
what does a zero primary deficit indicate
fiscal deficit is 5.6 and interest payments 3.6 percent of GDP, find the primary deficit
which deficit best shows the current fiscal stance
how are past debts kept out of the primary deficit measure

solution_steps.explain: Subtracting interest payments from the fiscal deficit leaves borrowing attributable to current spending alone.

worked_examples.question: Using Primary Deficit, compute the result for fiscal_deficit = 3, interest_payments = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Remove the legacy interest burden: primary_deficit = fiscal_deficit - interest_payments = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Primary Deficit, compute the result for fiscal_deficit = 4, interest_payments = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Remove the legacy interest burden: primary_deficit = fiscal_deficit - interest_payments = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Government Spending, Tax and Transfer Multipliers
concepts.definition: A rupee of public spending enters demand directly and multiplies through the MPC chain, while a rupee of tax change enters only through disposable income, so the tax multiplier is smaller in size and negative, and transfers work like taxes in reverse with a multiplier of c over one minus c.
concepts.key_idea: Spending hits demand at full strength, taxes and transfers only through the spending fraction, so their multipliers are one rung weaker.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, Box 5.1 fiscal policy, equations 5.5 to 5.8 and 5.21, pages 73-79
question_patterns: derive the government expenditure multiplier for a given marginal propensity to consume
compute the tax multiplier and explain its negative sign
why is the tax multiplier smaller in absolute size than the spending multiplier
find the income effect of a transfer payment change
government spending rises by 100 with MPC 0.8, find the change in equilibrium income
compare the income effects of a tax cut and an equal spending rise

solution_steps.action: Convert MPC into the saving leak
solution_steps.explain: The share of each extra rupee that leaks into saving governs every multiplier.

solution_steps.action: Invert the leak for the spending multiplier
solution_steps.explain: One over the saving fraction gives the government expenditure multiplier.

solution_steps.action: Weaken and flip for the tax multiplier
solution_steps.explain: Taxes act only through consumption, so the tax multiplier is minus the MPC over the MPS.

solution_steps.action: Scale transfers by the spending fraction
solution_steps.explain: A transfer change raises income by the MPC over the MPS times the transfer change, since part of any transfer is saved.

worked_examples.question: Using Government Spending, Tax and Transfer Multipliers, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert MPC into the saving leak: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = -2.0 Step 2: Invert the leak for the spending multiplier: government_spending_multiplier = 1 / marginal_propensity_to_save = -0.5 Step 3: Weaken and flip for the tax multiplier: tax_multiplier = -marginal_propensity_to_consume / marginal_propensity_to_save = 1.5 Step 4: Scale transfers by the spending fraction: transfer_multiplier = marginal_propensity_to_consume / marginal_propensity_to_save = -1.5 Final result: -1.5

worked_examples.question: Using Government Spending, Tax and Transfer Multipliers, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert MPC into the saving leak: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = -3.0 Step 2: Invert the leak for the spending multiplier: government_spending_multiplier = 1 / marginal_propensity_to_save = -0.333333 Step 3: Weaken and flip for the tax multiplier: tax_multiplier = -marginal_propensity_to_consume / marginal_propensity_to_save = 1.333333 Step 4: Scale transfers by the spending fraction: transfer_multiplier = marginal_propensity_to_consume / marginal_propensity_to_save = -1.333333 Final result: -1.333333

concepts.title: Balanced Budget Multiplier
concepts.definition: When an increase in government spending is financed by an equal rise in taxes, the spending and tax effects combine so that equilibrium income grows by exactly the extra spending - the balanced budget multiplier equals one.
concepts.key_idea: Equal rises in G and T lift income one-for-one, because the first-round tax leak skips the initial spending injection.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, Box 5.1, balanced budget multiplier, equations 5.9 to 5.13, pages 75-76
question_patterns: show that a balanced budget increase in G and T raises income by the same amount
why does the balanced budget multiplier equal unity
compute the combined income effect of equal rises in spending and taxes
government spending and taxes both rise by 100 with MPC 0.8, find the income change
add the two policy multipliers to obtain the balanced budget result
explain the first-round difference that leaves a net multiplier of one

solution_steps.explain: One over one minus c plus minus c over one minus c simplifies to exactly one.

solution_steps.action: Trace the rounds to see why
solution_steps.explain: Spending raises income from round one, while the tax rise bites only from round two through reduced consumption, so the chains differ by the initial injection.
A financed expansion is never neutral: output grows by the size of the extra spending even though the budget stays balanced.

concepts.title: Proportional Taxes and Automatic Stabilisers
concepts.definition: A proportional income tax of rate t trims the effective propensity to consume to c times one minus t, flattening aggregate demand and shrinking the multiplier; because collections rise in booms and fall in slumps, the tax acts as a built-in shock absorber without any policy decision.
concepts.key_idea: Proportional taxes dampen every upswing and cushion every downswing automatically.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, Box 5.1, proportional taxes, equations 5.14 to 5.20, automatic stabiliser discussion, pages 76-78
question_patterns: how does a proportional income tax change the size of the multiplier
compute the effective marginal propensity to consume under a tax rate
why is the proportional tax called an automatic stabiliser
find the spending multiplier when MPC is 0.8 and the tax rate is 0.25
distinguish automatic stabilisation from discretionary fiscal policy
what happens to disposable income in a recession with a proportional tax

solution_steps.action: Trim the spending fraction by the tax rate
solution_steps.explain: Of each extra rupee of income, the tax office takes t first, so consumption responds only to c times one minus t.
With a smaller effective slope the aggregate demand line is flatter and the multiplier falls - for MPC 0.8 and t 0.25 it drops from 5 to 2.5 - which is what steadies the cycle automatically.

worked_examples.question: Using Proportional Taxes and Automatic Stabilisers, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3, tax_rate = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Trim the spending fraction by the tax rate: effective_mpc = marginal_propensity_to_consume * (1 - tax_rate) = -6.0 Final result: -6.0

worked_examples.question: Using Proportional Taxes and Automatic Stabilisers, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 4, tax_rate = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Trim the spending fraction by the tax rate: effective_mpc = marginal_propensity_to_consume * (1 - tax_rate) = -12.0 Final result: -12.0

concepts.title: Government Debt, Ricardian Equivalence and Crowding Out
concepts.definition: Year after year of deficits accumulate into a debt stock whose interest itself adds to future deficits; whether debt is a burden turns on growth effects - Ricardian equivalence claims far-sighted savers offset public borrowing, while crowding out warns that government bonds soak up private savings.
concepts.key_idea: Deficits are flows feeding a debt stock, and the debate is whether that stock taxes future growth or rides on it.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec105.txt, Debt section, Ricardian equivalence and crowding out, pages 79-81
question_patterns: explain how deficits accumulate into government debt
what is Ricardian equivalence and why does it matter for debt policy
how does government borrowing crowd out private investment
does public debt always burden future generations
why is external debt treated as more burdensome than internal debt
when can deficit-financed growth make debt painless to carry

solution_steps.explain: Each year's deficit borrows, and unpaid interest joins the principal, so the debt stock compounds.
Borrowing can shift today's consumption onto future taxpayers and squeeze private capital formation, though growth financed by public investment can repay the debt.

Ricardian equivalence says far-sighted households save against future taxes, neutralising borrowing, while crowding out says bond sales compete away private funds - unless higher income enlarges the savings pool.

worked_examples.question_pattern: With MPC equal to 0.8, the government raises spending by 100. Find the spending multiplier, the tax multiplier, and the income effect of a transfer rise of 100.

solution_template.explain: One over 0.2 is 5, so income rises by 5 times 100, that is 500.
Minus 0.8 over 0.2 gives minus 4, so a 100 tax cut would raise income by 400.
0.8 over 0.2 gives 4, so a 100 transfer rise lifts income by 400.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Total expenditure is 15 percent of GDP, revenue receipts 9.2, recovery of loans 0.1 and disinvestment 0.1. Find the fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP.

solution_template.explain: 9.2 plus 0.1 plus 0.1 gives 9.4 percent of GDP.
15 minus 9.4 leaves 5.6 percent of GDP, the borrowing requirement.

worked_examples.question_pattern: MPC is 0.8 and a proportional income tax of 0.25 is imposed. Find the effective propensity to consume out of income.

solution_template.explain: 0.8 times one minus 0.25 gives 0.6, so the AD line flattens and the multiplier falls to one over one minus 0.6, that is 2.5.
